steps.title: Два способа сказать «сейчас уже не так»
steps.html:
She used to leave the house at ten past seven. — привычка, которой больше нет.

She would walk the same route every morning. — та же привычка, но внутри рассказа.

The pattern used to run… — прошлое состояние, не привычка. Здесь возможно только used to.

steps.title: В каком предложении нельзя использовать would?
options: She left the house at seven every morning.
We had a factory in this street.
He walked the same route to work.
steps.answer: We had a factory in this street.
steps.why: Have здесь — состояние, а не повторяющееся действие. Можно used to have, но не would have.

steps.title: used to, would, Past Simple
steps.html:
ФормаКогда используемПример
used to + verbповторявшаяся привычка, теперь законченнаяShe used to leave at ten past seven.
used to + verbпрошлое состояние, которого больше нетThere used to be a factory here.
would + verbповторявшаяся привычка — но не состояниеShe would walk the same route every morning.
past simpleединичное событие или всё то же с указанием времениShe retired in 2004.
didn't use to / Did you use to…?отрицание и вопрос — обратите внимание на написаниеShe didn't use to question them.

steps.title: Как это работает
steps.html:
Обе формы говорят одно: это повторялось и больше не повторяется. Там, где речь о привычке, они взаимозаменяемы.

Разница — в состоянии. Used to подходит для состояний — I used to have a car. Would — нет.

Would к тому же требует, чтобы прошлое уже было задано. Рассказ не начинают с I would walk to school — начинают с used to, а дальше идёт would.

Есть второе used to, и это другое: be used to + -ing — «привык». I'm used to working late — про настоящее, не про прошлое.

She would walk the same route every morning.
There used to be a factory at the end of the street.
She didn't use to question the rules.
Did you use to work at weekends?

steps.title: The way we used to work
steps.html:
Прочитайте один раз. Автор отказывается вставать на чью-то сторону — найдите это место.

My grandmother worked in the same building for thirty-one years. She used to leave the house at ten past seven, and she would walk the same route every morning, past the entrance of the factory where her own mother had worked. When she retired they gave her a clock. She still has it.

Almost nothing about that is normal now. The job for life has gone; so has the single employer, and in most fields so has the idea that you stay in one city. A young architect who is made redundant in Athens does not wait for the local market to recover — she retrains as a landscape designer in Melbourne, because that is where the work is. The pattern used to run from the poorer country to the richer one. In recent years thousands of young Europeans have moved the other way, to Africa, Asia and South America, and they are not going as volunteers. They are going because the prospects are better there.

Some of what we lost was worth losing. My grandmother had no sick pay for the first eleven years, and there were procedures nobody would explain to her because she was not expected to ask. She used to obey the rules; she did not use to question them. Nobody in her office would have described the atmosphere as relaxed.

But something has gone with it. The people I know who move every two years have a wider life and a thinner one. They have seen more, and they belong to less. When I ask them what they will do at sixty, most of them laugh, which is the answer.

Things are not like they used to be, and that sentence is neither a complaint nor a compliment. It is just true, and the interesting question is what we are going to build in place of the clock.

A young architect who is made redundant in Athens does not wait for the local market to recover — she retrains as a landscape designer in Melbourne, because that is where the work is. The pattern used to run from the poorer country to the richer one. In recent years thousands of young Europeans have moved the other way, to Africa, Asia and South America, and they are not going as volunteers. They are going because the prospects are better there.

Some of what we lost was worth losing. My grandmother had no sick pay for the first eleven years, and there were procedures nobody would explain to her because she was not expected to ask. She used to obey the rules; she did not use to question them. Nobody in her office would have described the atmosphere as relaxed.

But something has gone with it. The people I know who move every two years have a wider life and a thinner one. They have seen more, and they belong to less. When I ask them what they will do at sixty, most of them laugh, which is the answer.

Things are not like they used to be, and that sentence is neither a complaint nor a compliment. It is just true, and the interesting question is what we are going to build in place of the clock.

steps.title: Как говорить о том, чего больше нет

items.text: Things aren't like they used to be.

steps.title: Ответьте вслух.
items: Опишите, как работал кто-то из вашей семьи поколение назад.
Что раньше было обычным на работе, а теперь нет?
Согласились бы вы на работу за границей? Что бы вы приобрели и потеряли?

steps.title: Теперь расскажите одним высказыванием. Запишите себя.
steps.sub: Used to — для состояний, would — для повторяющихся действий.
items: My … used to work … . In those days there used to be … .
Things aren't like they used to be: now … .

steps.title: Урок 19 пройден
items: Я говорю о законченных привычках и состояниях.
Я знаю, когда возможен would, а когда только used to.
Я могу говорить о работе и условиях труда.
Я при этом использую придаточные определительные.
